tagline: The book of Israel's rescue from slavery in Egypt, the covenant God makes with them at Mount Sinai, and the tent where he comes to live among them.
overview:
Exodus begins with a family that has become a nation and a nation that has become a slave people. The seventy descendants of Jacob who went down to Egypt at the end of Genesis have multiplied, and a new Pharaoh, afraid of their numbers, puts them to forced labor and orders their baby boys drowned. God raises up Moses, a Hebrew child pulled from the Nile and raised in Pharaoh's household, calls him from a burning bush in the wilderness, and reveals his name. Through ten plagues God breaks Pharaoh's grip, and on the night of the Passover he brings Israel out. At the sea he destroys Pharaoh's army, and in the desert he feeds his people with manna and gives them water from the rock.

The second half of the book takes place almost entirely at Mount Sinai. There God makes a covenant (a binding, sworn relationship with obligations on both sides) with the people he has rescued, gives them the Ten Commandments and a body of laws, and gives detailed instructions for a portable sanctuary, the tabernacle, where he will dwell among them. Almost at once the people break the covenant by worshiping a golden calf. Moses intercedes, God renews the covenant and proclaims his own character, and the book ends with the tabernacle built and the glory of the LORD filling it.

Exodus is the Old Testament's central story of salvation. Psalmists, prophets, and apostles return to it again and again to explain what God is like and what it means to be rescued by him. Its movement is from slavery to worship. Israel is freed from serving Pharaoh in order to serve the LORD, and the story does not end on the far shore of the sea but on the day God comes to live with his people.
author:
Exodus, like the rest of the Pentateuch (the first five books of the Bible, called the Torah in Jewish tradition), does not name its author. Jewish and Christian tradition has long held that Moses wrote it, and the book itself says Moses wrote down particular material: the record against Amalek (17:14), the words of the LORD at the covenant ceremony (24:4), and the words of the renewed covenant (34:27). Jesus refers to the account of the burning bush as part of the book of Moses (Mark 12:26). Many conservative scholars hold that Moses is the substantial source of the book, while allowing for later editing such as the updating of place names.

Since the nineteenth century many critical scholars have instead seen the Pentateuch as woven together from several sources written over centuries. The classic form of that view, the Documentary Hypothesis associated with Julius Wellhausen, identified four sources (usually labeled J, E, D, and P) and dated the priestly material, which includes much of the tabernacle section, to the time of the Babylonian exile or after. Many scholars have since moved away from the neat four-source scheme toward other models, often distinguishing simply between priestly and non-priestly material, and the debate about how and when the book reached its final form continues. Readers across these views agree that Exodus as we have it is a carefully shaped whole.
date:
Two dates matter here: when the events happened and when the book was written. For the exodus itself, two main dates are proposed. The earlier date, around 1446 BC, comes from counting back from 1 Kings 6:1, which places the exodus 480 years before the fourth year of Solomon's reign (about 966 BC). The later date, in the thirteenth century BC and often under Ramesses II (who reigned about 1279 to 1213 BC), rests on the name of the store city Rameses in Exodus 1:11 and on the pattern of new village settlement in the hill country of Canaan around 1200 BC; its defenders read the 480 years as a round figure for twelve generations. The earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible, on the victory stela of Pharaoh Merneptah from around 1208 BC, names Israel as a people already living in Canaan. Some scholars doubt that the exodus happened as described, or think the escape of a smaller group grew into the story of the whole nation. No Egyptian record mentions the event, which defenders of its history note is unsurprising, since Egyptian royal inscriptions rarely if ever recorded defeats.

The date of writing follows from a reader's view of authorship: the time of Moses on the traditional view, and anywhere from the early monarchy to the Persian period (the fifth century BC) for the book's final form on various critical views.
setting:
Exodus opens in the eastern Nile Delta, the region Genesis calls Goshen, where Egypt met the land bridge to Canaan. Egypt was the great power of the age. Its king, the Pharaoh, was regarded as a son of the sun god and the earthly embodiment of the god Horus, and its wealth rested on the yearly flooding of the Nile and on vast building projects carried out by conscripted and foreign labor. The book never names the Pharaoh of the oppression or of the exodus; it calls him only by his title. Semitic peoples from Canaan are well attested in the Delta through the second millennium BC. A line of foreign rulers known as the Hyksos governed northern Egypt for about a century before being driven out around 1550 BC, and some scholars connect the new king who did not know Joseph with the suspicion of foreigners that followed.

After leaving Egypt, Israel moves through the wilderness of the Sinai Peninsula to the mountain of God, called both Sinai and Horeb. Its location is debated. Christian tradition since late antiquity has identified it with Jebel Musa in the southern peninsula, while others propose sites in the northern Sinai or in northwest Arabia, the region of Midian. The first readers were Israelites who needed to know who they were, where they had come from, and which God had claimed them, whether they first heard the book on the edge of the promised land, under the kings, or rebuilding after exile.
purpose: Exodus tells Israel who its God is and who they are because of what he has done. It explains the origin of the Passover, the Sabbath as a sign of the covenant, the priesthood, and the tabernacle, and it grounds Israel's law in a rescue. The Ten Commandments open with the words “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” Obedience is the response of a freed people, not the price of freedom. The book also warns, through the golden calf, how quickly a rescued people can make a god of its own, and it shows that Israel's survival depends on a God who forgives and still goes with them.
story: Exodus picks up where Genesis ends. Genesis closes with Jacob's family settled in Egypt and Joseph's dying promise that God would bring them up to the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Exodus shows the first part of God's promise to Abraham (a great nation) fulfilled even under oppression, and the rescue begins because God remembers his covenant with the patriarchs. The book ends with God dwelling in the tabernacle at Sinai, which leads straight into Leviticus, where God speaks from that tent and teaches a sinful people how to live near a holy God. Numbers then carries them from Sinai through forty years in the wilderness to the edge of Canaan. Across the rest of the Bible the exodus becomes the pattern for every later rescue. The prophets describe the return from Babylon as a new exodus (especially in Isaiah 40 to 55), and the New Testament describes the work of Jesus in its language.
christ: The New Testament reads the exodus as the pattern that Jesus fills. Jesus died at Passover, and at the Last Supper, a Passover meal, he spoke of the cup as his blood of the covenant, echoing the covenant blood Moses sprinkled on the people in Exodus 24:8. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and John notes that none of Jesus' bones were broken, recalling the rule for the Passover lamb in Exodus 12:46 (John 19:36). At the transfiguration, Luke says Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure, using the Greek word exodos (Luke 9:31). John says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, using a verb built on the word for a tent, and that his glory was seen, as the glory once filled the tabernacle (John 1:14). Jesus calls himself the true bread from heaven, greater than the manna (John 6), and his “I am” sayings in John's Gospel are widely read against the name revealed at the bush. Hebrews reads the tabernacle and its priesthood as copies and shadows of the heavenly reality that Christ has entered (Hebrews 8 to 10). Exodus itself does not name a Messiah; what it gives the church are the categories (redemption, the lamb, covenant blood, God dwelling among his people, glory) in which it learned to understand him.
reading:
Exodus combines several kinds of writing: narrative (chapters 1 to 19 and 32 to 34), law (chapters 20 to 23), and detailed instructions and building reports for the tabernacle (chapters 25 to 31 and 35 to 40). Readers often hurry through the tabernacle chapters, but their length is part of the point. The book gives as much space to God's dwelling as to Israel's rescue, and the building report largely repeats the instructions to show the people doing exactly what God said. Watch for repeated phrases: God hearing the cry of the oppressed, the refrain that Egypt and Israel will know that he is the LORD, and the verb serve, since the same Hebrew root describes slavery to Pharaoh and the worship of God.

A few misreadings are common. The laws are not a ladder by which Israel earned God's favor; they are given to people already rescued. The plagues are neither random natural disasters nor mere magic; the text presents them as judgments on the gods of Egypt (12:12). And the hardening of Pharaoh's heart should be read alongside the verses that say Pharaoh hardened his own heart. The large numbers in the book (600,000 men on foot in 12:37) are also debated. Some take them at face value, while others argue that the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a clan or a military unit, which would make the company much smaller.

structure.title: Oppression in Egypt and the birth of Moses
structure.summary: Jacob's descendants multiply in Egypt, and a fearful Pharaoh enslaves them and orders their sons killed. Moses is saved from the Nile, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, and flees to Midian after killing an Egyptian. God hears Israel's cry.

structure.title: The call of Moses
structure.summary: God appears to Moses in a burning bush, reveals his name, and sends him to Pharaoh. Moses resists, Aaron is given as his spokesman, and the first demand to Pharaoh only makes the slavery worse. God renews his promise to redeem his people.

structure.title: The plagues on Egypt
structure.summary: In a series of escalating plagues, from the Nile turned to blood to three days of darkness, God shows his power over Egypt and its gods while Pharaoh repeatedly refuses to let Israel go. The death of the firstborn is announced.

structure.title: Passover, the exodus, and the sea
structure.summary: Israel keeps the first Passover, the firstborn of Egypt die, and Pharaoh drives the people out. God leads them by pillars of cloud and fire, divides the sea for Israel, and brings the waters back on Pharaoh's army. Moses and Miriam lead a song of praise.

structure.title: Through the wilderness to Sinai
structure.summary: In the desert the people grumble over water and food, and God provides sweet water, quail, manna, and water from the rock. Israel defeats Amalek, and Jethro counsels Moses to share the work of judging the people.

structure.title: The covenant at Sinai
structure.summary: At the mountain God offers Israel a covenant, speaks the Ten Commandments, and gives the laws of the Book of the Covenant. The people agree, the covenant is sealed with blood, and Israel's leaders see the God of Israel and eat in his presence.

structure.title: Instructions for the tabernacle
structure.summary: On the mountain God gives Moses the pattern for the tabernacle, its furniture, the priests' garments, and the ordination of Aaron and his sons, closing with the Sabbath as the sign of the covenant.

structure.title: The golden calf and the covenant renewed
structure.summary: While Moses is on the mountain the people worship a golden calf. Moses intercedes, God refuses to abandon them, reveals his goodness to Moses, proclaims his character, and renews the covenant.

structure.title: The tabernacle built and filled
structure.summary: The people give generously, and skilled workers build the tabernacle exactly as commanded. Moses sets it up, and the cloud covers it as the glory of the LORD fills the tent.

themes.title: The God who hears and remembers
themes.body: The rescue begins not with Israel's faith but with God's attention. When the Israelites groan under slavery, the text says that God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (2:24), and at the bush he tells Moses that he has seen their affliction and heard their cry (3:7). Remembering in the Bible is not recalling something forgotten; it means acting on a commitment. Exodus presents a God who is moved by the suffering of the powerless and keeps his promises across centuries.

themes.title: From slavery to service
themes.body: The same Hebrew root, avad, means to serve as a slave and to serve God in worship. Pharaoh makes Israel serve him ruthlessly; God's repeated demand is that Pharaoh let his people go so that they may serve him. Exodus is not a story of freedom as independence. It is a change of masters, from a king who crushes to a God who gives rest, law, and his own presence.

themes.title: Knowing the LORD
themes.body: The book turns on a name. At the bush God reveals himself as I AM and as the LORD (the divine name, usually written YHWH), and the plagues are sent so that Egypt and Israel will know that he is the LORD. Pharaoh begins by asking who the LORD is that he should obey him (5:2). By the end of the book God proclaims his own character to Moses: “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (34:6), words the rest of the Old Testament quotes again and again.

themes.title: Covenant and law
themes.body: At Sinai God binds himself to Israel and Israel to him, calling them to be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (19:6), a people who would show the nations what God is like. The law that follows covers worship, family, property, justice for the poor and the stranger, and the rhythm of Sabbath. It is given after the rescue, as the shape of life for people who belong to a holy God, and it assumes that failure will need forgiveness.

themes.title: God dwelling among his people
themes.body: The book's last third is about a tent. God's goal is not only to bring Israel out of Egypt but to bring them to himself and live among them. The golden calf nearly ends that hope, and Moses pleads that if God's presence does not go with them there is no point in going on (33:15). The book ends with the answer: “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (40:34). The holiness that makes God dangerous and the mercy that makes him near are held together in that tent.

keyChapters.why: God appears in the burning bush, hears the cry of his people, sends Moses, and reveals his name, I AM WHO I AM.
The first Passover: the lamb, the blood on the doorframes, the death of Egypt's firstborn, and the night Israel goes free.
God divides the sea for Israel and destroys Pharaoh's army, the Old Testament's defining act of salvation.
At Sinai God offers the covenant and calls Israel to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, then descends on the mountain in fire.
The Ten Commandments, grounded in the words that open them: the LORD who brought Israel out of the house of slavery.
The golden calf, Israel's first great breach of the covenant, and Moses' intercession for the people.
God proclaims his name and character to Moses and renews the broken covenant, a passage quoted throughout the Old Testament.
The tabernacle is set up and the glory of the LORD fills it, the goal toward which the whole book moves.

parts.body:
Exodus is the second book of the Bible. It has 40 chapters. It tells how God rescued the people of Israel from slavery in Egypt, made a covenant with them at Mount Sinai, and came to live among them in a tent.

The book opens where Genesis ended. Jacob's family, seventy people in all (1:5), had gone down to Egypt in a famine. Now they have grown into a great people, and a new king is afraid of them. He makes them slaves and orders their baby boys thrown into the Nile. One boy, Moses, is drawn out of the river and raised in Pharaoh's own house. Years later, keeping sheep in the desert, he sees a bush that burns and is not burned up, and God speaks to him from it.

What follows is one of the great stories of the world. Moses goes back to Egypt. Ten plagues fall. On the night of the first Passover Israel goes free. God opens a way through the sea, feeds the people with manna in the desert, and brings them to his mountain. There he gives them the Ten Commandments and makes them his own people. Almost at once they make a golden calf and worship it. Moses pleads for them, God forgives, and the book ends with the tent of worship built and ‘the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle’ (40:34).

The book moves from slavery to worship. One Hebrew word can mean both to serve a master as a slave and to serve God in worship. Israel is not set free to belong to no one. It is set free from a king who crushed it, to belong to a God who hears the cry of the oppressed. The rest of the Bible keeps coming back to this story to say what God is like and what it means to be rescued by him.

parts.h: The second book of the Torah
parts.body:
Exodus is the second of the five books that Jews call the Torah, a word that means ‘teaching’ or ‘instruction’. Christians often call the same five books the Pentateuch. In Jewish tradition the book is called Shemot, ‘Names’, from its opening words: “These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob” (1:1). Its English name comes from the Greek word exodos, which means a way out, or departure.

The book is joined to Genesis on purpose. Genesis began with God's blessing on the first humans: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). Exodus opens with that blessing come true in one family: “the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous, so that the land was filled with them” (1:7). Genesis ended with Joseph's dying promise that God would bring his people back to the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Exodus begins with that promise still waiting, and with God who remembers it: “God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (2:24).

Exodus also leads on. It ends with God living in the tabernacle at Sinai. The next book, Leviticus, begins with God speaking from that tent and teaching a people how to live near a holy God. Numbers carries them through the wilderness to the edge of Canaan, and Deuteronomy gives Moses' last words before they cross the Jordan. Exodus is the center of the five, the book in which a family becomes a nation that belongs to God.

parts.h: Who wrote it, and how we know
parts.body:
Exodus does not name its author. Jewish and Christian tradition has long held that Moses wrote it, with the rest of the Torah. The book itself says that Moses wrote down some things: the record against Amalek (17:14), the words of the LORD at the covenant ceremony (24:4), and the words of the renewed covenant (34:27). Jesus speaks of the scene at the burning bush as part of “the Book of Moses” (Mark 12:26). Many conservative scholars hold that Moses is the main source of the book, while allowing for later editing, such as old place names brought up to date.

Since the nineteenth century many critical scholars have seen the Torah as woven from several written sources over centuries. The classic form of that view, linked with the German scholar Julius Wellhausen, named four sources, usually given the letters J, E, D and P. It dated the priestly material, which includes much of the tabernacle section, to the time of the exile in Babylon or after. Many scholars have since moved away from the neat four-source scheme. Some now speak simply of ‘priestly’ and ‘non-priestly’ material, and the debate about how and when the book reached its final form goes on.

These views give different answers to when the book was written: in the time of Moses on the traditional view, and on various critical views anywhere from the early days of Israel's kings to the Persian period, after the exile. Readers across all these views agree on one thing. Exodus as we have it is a carefully shaped whole, and it should be read as one. Christians who confess the Bible as God's word hold more than one of these views. These notes do not settle the question, and the book's authority does not hang on knowing the writer's name.

Exodus never names a year, and it never names the Pharaoh. It calls him only by his title. So the date has to be worked out, and two main dates are proposed.

The early date. 1 Kings 6:1 says that Solomon began to build the temple “In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt”, in the fourth year of his reign. Solomon's fourth year is usually placed about 966 BC. Counting back 480 years gives about 1446 BC, in the fifteenth century BC. On this view the Pharaoh Moses faced reigned in the 1400s; Thutmose III and Amenhotep II are the names usually given.

The later date. Others place the exodus in the thirteenth century BC, often under Ramesses II, who reigned about 1279 to 1213 BC. They point to the store city called Rameses in 1:11, and to the many new villages that appear in the hill country of Canaan around 1200 BC. On this view the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 are a round figure for twelve generations of forty years. Those who hold the early date reply that the name Rameses may be an older place name brought up to date by a later hand, as in Genesis 47:11.

What is fixed. On a victory stone set up by Pharaoh Merneptah about 1208 BC, Israel is named as a people already living in Canaan. It is the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible. On either date, then, Israel was in the land by the end of the thirteenth century.

Those who doubt. Some scholars doubt that the exodus happened as Exodus tells it. Some think the escape of a smaller group grew, in the telling, into the story of the whole nation. Others see the book as a later national epic. No Egyptian record mentions the plagues or Israel's leaving. Those who defend the story's history answer that Egypt's royal inscriptions rarely if ever recorded a defeat. They point to details that fit Egypt well: Semitic peoples living in the eastern Nile Delta, foreign workers on royal building works, and Egyptian names in the family of Levi, Moses' own family, among them Phinehas, which means ‘the Nubian’.

Christians who hold the Bible as God's word are found on both sides of the date, and they differ too on how to read the numbers of people who left (see the part on the sea, the road and the mountain, below). These notes take no side on the date. What the book cares about is not the year but the God who heard a cry and came down to rescue.

Exodus opens in the eastern Nile Delta, the region Genesis calls Goshen, where Egypt met the land bridge to Canaan. Egypt was the great power of the age. Its wealth rested on the yearly flooding of the Nile and on great building works carried out by conscripted and foreign workers. Its king, the Pharaoh, was honored as a son of the sun god and as the god Horus on earth.

Peoples from Canaan are known to have lived in the Delta through the second millennium BC. A line of foreign rulers called the Hyksos governed northern Egypt for about a century before they were driven out around 1550 BC. Some scholars link ‘a new king, who did not know Joseph’ (1:8) with the suspicion of foreigners that followed.

The king's fear is plain in his own words. Israel has become ‘too numerous and too powerful for us’ (1:9), and ‘if a war breaks out, they may join our enemies’ (1:10). Fear of a people inside the land turns into forced labor, then into killing. Exodus watches that slide closely, and it is honest about it. The story is told from the side of the slaves.

But Exodus is not a story against Egyptians as a people. Pharaoh's own daughter pities a Hebrew baby and saves him (2:6). Some of Pharaoh's officials ‘feared the word of the LORD’ and brought their servants and animals in from the hail (9:20). Many Egyptians showed Israel favor (11:3), and a ‘mixed multitude’ went out with Israel (12:38). Israel's law later told the people, “Do not despise an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land” (Deuteronomy 23:7). The prophet Isaiah looked ahead to a day when “Egypt will acknowledge the LORD” and worship him (Isaiah 19:21). The God who judged Pharaoh did not stop intending good for Egypt.

Exodus has three main movements, and each one is a different kind of writing.

Chapters 1 to 18 are story: the slavery, the birth and call of Moses, the plagues, the Passover, the crossing of the sea, and the first weeks in the wilderness, with grumbling over water and food and God's patient answers. Chapters 19 to 24 are covenant: Israel arrives at Mount Sinai, God speaks the Ten Commandments, and he gives a body of laws called the Book of the Covenant (chapters 21 to 23). The covenant is sealed with blood in chapter 24. Chapters 25 to 40 are about God's dwelling. God gives Moses the plans for the tabernacle and its priests (25 to 31). Then the golden calf breaks the covenant, and Moses pleads for the people (32 to 34). Last, the tabernacle is built exactly as God commanded, and his glory fills it (35 to 40).

Readers often hurry through the tabernacle chapters, but their length is part of the point. The book gives as much room to God's dwelling as to Israel's rescue. The building report repeats the instructions almost word for word, to show the people doing just what God said.

Some phrases come back again and again. God hears the cry of the oppressed. Egypt and Israel will ‘know that I am the LORD’ (7:5; 6:7). And the verb ‘serve’ runs through the book, because the same Hebrew root describes slavery to Pharaoh and the worship of God. Pharaoh asks, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go?” (5:2). The rest of the book is the answer.

At the burning bush Moses asks what he should say when the people ask God's name. God answers, “I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” (3:14). Then he gives the name itself: ‘The LORD, the God of your fathers’ (3:15).

The Hebrew of ‘I AM WHO I AM’ is ehyeh asher ehyeh. It is built from the verb ‘to be’. Because the Hebrew verb covers present and future, it can also be translated with the future: I will be what I will be. Only two verses earlier, God used the same word for a promise: ‘I will surely be with you’ (3:12). Readers have heard three things in the name, and they fit together. God simply is: he depends on nothing. God is free: no one can define him or control him. And God will be there: he will be with his people. In Exodus the third comes first, because the name is given as a promise to slaves.

The name itself is four Hebrew letters, YHWH, probably said ‘Yahweh’. Out of reverence Jews came to avoid saying it aloud and read Adonai, ‘Lord’, in its place. Most English Bibles follow that custom by printing it LORD in small capitals.

A puzzle follows in 6:3. God says, “I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty, but by My name the LORD I did not make Myself known to them.” Yet Genesis uses the name often. Three main answers are given. Many critical scholars see two traditions here, one in which the name was first given to Moses and one in which it was known from the start. Many Jewish and Christian interpreters argue that to ‘know’ a name in the Bible means to know by experience what it stands for. The patriarchs used the name but never saw the promises kept; Israel is about to learn what the name means as God redeems them. A third, smaller group thinks the narrator of Genesis, writing later, used the name for the God the patriarchs called God Almighty. Each view takes the text seriously. The chapter's own claim is clear: the God who speaks is the God who promised Abraham, now making himself known in a new way.

Ten plagues fall on Egypt, from the Nile turned to blood to the death of the firstborn. They are not presented as random disasters or as magic. God says that on the last night “I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt” (12:12). Egyptians honored the Nile's yearly flood as the god Hapi. The sun god Re was among the greatest of their gods, and one of Pharaoh's titles was Son of Re. Some cattle were sacred. One by one the powers Egypt trusted are shown to be helpless before the LORD who made them.

The hardening of Pharaoh's heart. Exodus says it in three ways. Before the plagues begin, God says, “I will harden his heart” (4:21). Then the text says simply that Pharaoh's heart was hard, without naming a cause (7:13). It says Pharaoh ‘hardened his heart’ himself (8:15). And from the sixth plague on, it says “the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (9:12). Through the first five plagues the narrator never says God did it. Pharaoh's own resistance comes first. The Hebrew uses three verbs: one means to make strong, one to make heavy, one to make hard.

Christians read this in more than one way. Many in the Reformed tradition, following Paul in Romans 9, hold that God's sovereign purpose stands behind Pharaoh's choices without making them any less his own, so that he remains fully guilty. Paul writes, “He hardens whom He wants to harden” (Romans 9:18). Many in the Arminian tradition, and many Jewish readers, stress that Pharaoh hardened himself first, and that God's hardening was a judgment that confirmed the road Pharaoh had chosen. Some add that God kept Pharaoh from simply giving way in fear, so that his choices showed what was truly in his heart. Both readings agree that Pharaoh is never pictured as a man who wanted to do right and was stopped. This is a question on which faithful Christians differ, and these notes take no side.

The death of the firstborn. The last plague is the hardest page in the book. Every firstborn son in Egypt dies, ‘from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon’ (12:29). The book sets it after Pharaoh's own order to drown Israel's sons (1:22), after God's warning to him (4:22-23), and after nine plagues and many chances to relent. It does not make the night small. The text says there was “loud wailing in Egypt; for there was no house without someone dead” (12:30). Jewish tradition has grieved for Egypt's dead: a well-known teaching in the Talmud tells of God silencing the angels who wanted to sing as the Egyptians drowned, because the work of his hands was dying. Some thoughtful Christians admit that this remains a place where they must trust what they cannot fully see. Behind every one of those doors was a mother. If you have lost a child, or carry a grief like hers, please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. The chapter notes on Exodus 11 and 12 face the question at more length.

On the night before Israel left, each household killed a lamb, put its blood on the doorframes of the house, and ate the meat roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, dressed to travel. God said, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (12:13). The name of the feast, Pesach in Hebrew, comes from that verb, to pass over. Israel's firstborn were not spared because they were better than the Egyptians. They were spared under the blood, by God's promise.

The night was to be remembered for ever: “this day will be a memorial for you, and you are to celebrate it as a feast to the LORD, as a permanent statute for the generations to come” (12:14). The feast was built around children's questions: “When your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’” (12:26). Exodus tells parents to answer with the story.

Passover is not only a feast in an old book. Jewish families still keep it today. After the temple was destroyed in AD 70, lambs could no longer be sacrificed, and the Seder became the Jewish form of the feast: four cups of wine, the children's questions, and a retelling that begins in shame and ends in praise. A roasted bone on the Seder plate recalls the lamb. The Haggadah, the order of the meal, builds its teaching of four kinds of children on the questions in the Torah. Christians should speak of this living observance with respect. It is the Jewish people's own remembrance of what God did for them.

Christians also see Jesus in this night, because the New Testament draws the line itself. Jesus died at Passover. At his last meal he said of the cup, “This is My blood of the covenant” (Mark 14:24). Paul writes, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). John notes that none of Jesus' bones were broken, recalling the rule for the Passover lamb (John 19:36; Exodus 12:46). For Christians the Lord's Supper grew from that meal. None of this takes Passover away from the Jewish people or empties it. The story belonged to Israel first, and it still does.

parts.h: The sea, the road and the mountain
parts.body:
The sea. English Bibles call it the Red Sea. The Hebrew is yam suph, which means sea of reeds. The Bible uses the name for the Gulf of Suez and for the Gulf of Aqaba (1 Kings 9:26), and perhaps also for marshy lakes nearer Egypt. Where Israel crossed is not known. The places proposed include the Gulf of Suez, the Bitter Lakes or Lake Timsah along the line of the modern Suez Canal, a lagoon on the Mediterranean coast, and the Gulf of Aqaba. The place names in 14:2 have not been securely located. The text itself names a means: ‘a strong east wind’ that blew ‘all that night’ (14:21). Readers hold a range of views, from those who take the account as it stands, to those who look for natural means God used, to those who read it as Israel's later, poetic memory of its beginning.

The road. God did not lead the people along the coast road ‘through the land of the Philistines, though it was shorter’ (13:17). That was the main route to Canaan, and Egypt guarded it with forts. The camps that follow, Succoth, Etham, Marah, Elim and Rephidim, have not been located with certainty, though Succoth is often placed in a valley leading east from the Delta. No route is drawn on the map with this book for that reason.

The mountain. Mount Sinai, also called Horeb, has not been found by archaeology. Christian tradition since at least the fourth century has placed it at Jebel Musa, Arabic for the mountain of Moses, in the south of the Sinai Peninsula, where a monastery stands. Others propose peaks in the north of the peninsula, or sites in northwest Arabia, the land of Midian. Paul's phrase ‘Mount Sinai in Arabia’ (Galatians 4:25) is cited in that debate, though the name Arabia was used loosely in his day.

How many left? Exodus says “about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children” (12:37). With families that would be two million or more. Some take the number as written, noting that it agrees with the totals in Numbers. Others note that the Hebrew word elef, ‘thousand’, can also mean a clan or a military unit, as in Judges 6:15, where Gideon calls his ‘clan’ the weakest in Manasseh, and that read this way the company would be far smaller. Each reading has its difficulty. Christians who hold Scripture as God's word are found on both sides, and these notes take no side.

Israel is not given the law in Egypt. It is given at Sinai, to people already set free. The Ten Commandments open, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (20:2). Exodus gives nineteen chapters of rescue before the first commandment. Law follows grace in the order of the text. Israel is not told to obey in order to be rescued. It is told to live as a people already rescued.

Before the law, God offers a covenant. A covenant is a binding, sworn relationship with promises and duties on both sides. God reminds the people, “I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself” (19:4), and calls them to be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (19:6): a people who would show the nations what God is like.

The Bible never numbers the commandments. It calls them the ‘ten words’ (34:28), and traditions count them differently. Jewish tradition counts 20:2, ‘I am the LORD your God’, as the first word, and joins other gods and images as the second. Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, join other gods and images as the first commandment and divide coveting into two. Orthodox and Reformed Christians, following an older division found in the Jewish writers Philo and Josephus, count other gods and images as two commandments. The words are the same in every tradition; only the count differs.

After the ten comes the Book of the Covenant (chapters 21 to 23), laws for worship, family, property, and justice for the poor and the stranger. Some of these laws are hard for a modern reader, among them laws about servants and slaves. The chapter notes face them one by one, and these notes do not defend slavery. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used texts like these to defend slavery as biblical. That was a misuse of Scripture. Israel's own law kept reminding the people that they had been slaves themselves.

parts.h: The tent, the calf, and the name proclaimed
parts.body:
God tells Moses, “they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them” (25:8). The Hebrew word for the tabernacle, mishkan, means a dwelling place. God's goal was not only to bring Israel out of Egypt but to bring them to himself and live among them. The tent could be taken down and carried as the people traveled.

While Moses is on the mountain receiving those plans, the people make a golden calf and say it brought them out of Egypt. It is the first great breaking of the covenant, and it comes only weeks after the people had promised to do all that God said. Exodus does not hide it. The people's gold went into the calf, and later, freely given, into the tabernacle.

Moses pleads for the people. God refuses to abandon them, and Moses says, “If Your Presence does not go with us” ... “do not lead us up from here” (33:15). Then God passes before Moses and proclaims his own name: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (34:6). These words are quoted again and again in the rest of the Old Testament. They are said in Exodus right after Israel's worst failure.

The book ends with the tent finished. “Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (40:34). The holiness that makes God dangerous and the mercy that makes him near are held together in that tent.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Exodus
parts.body:
The New Testament comes back to Exodus often, and it draws its own lines from the story to Jesus. These lines do not take the story's meaning away from Israel. They say that the God who rescued Israel has acted again.

John writes, “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory” (John 1:14). The verb for ‘made His dwelling’ is built on the Greek word for a tent, and ‘glory’ is the word for what filled the tabernacle. A few verses later John says, “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

Paul calls Jesus “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). In 1 Corinthians 10 he retells the wilderness years. The people ‘passed through the sea’ and ate and drank what God gave, “and that rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Yet most of them fell in the wilderness. “these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Paul does not tell the story against Israel. He tells it to the church, as a warning to the church.

Hebrews sets Moses beside Jesus: “Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house” (Hebrews 3:5), and Christ is faithful ‘as the Son over God’s house’ (Hebrews 3:6). Hebrews 8 to 10 read the tabernacle as ‘a copy and shadow of what is in heaven’ (Hebrews 8:5), and see Christ entering the true sanctuary ‘by His own blood’ (Hebrews 9:12).

Luke says that at the transfiguration Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his ‘departure’ (Luke 9:31); the Greek word is exodos. And Jesus says that the true bread from heaven is given by his Father, and that he is ‘the bread of life’ (John 6:32-35).

One thing must be said plainly. For centuries some Christians used the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why. Exodus is the Jewish people's own story of rescue. Christians who read it are reading a story they share with them.

parts.h: How Jews and Christians have read it
parts.body:
Exodus is Israel's Scripture first, and it stands at the heart of Jewish life. Its story is retold at every Passover. Its commandments were recited daily in the temple with the Shema, according to the Mishnah. Later Jewish tradition linked the giving of the law at Sinai with the Feast of Weeks, Shavuot, fifty days after Passover, so that the feast came to celebrate the gift of the Torah. In the synagogue it is read week by week, in order.

The earliest evidence of Passover outside the Bible comes from Elephantine, a Jewish military colony on the Nile in southern Egypt. In a letter of about 419 BC the colony is told to keep the festival of unleavened bread from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of the month, and to keep leaven out of their houses.

Christian readers have read Exodus in many ways. In his Life of Moses, Gregory of Nyssa read Moses' longing to see God's glory as the soul's endless climb toward a God who is always more than can be seen. Origen and Augustine read the gold Israel carried out of Egypt as a picture of learning that Christians could take from the pagan world and put to God's service. The great Christian festival of Easter grew from Passover, and in many languages its name still comes from the Hebrew pesach.

The story has also given words to people in chains. The spiritual Go Down, Moses, first published from the singing of escaped slaves in 1861, took up God's hearing of his people's cry. People who suffer have often found in Exodus a God who sees affliction and does not look away.

The book itself teaches how to carry such a memory. Israel was not told to use its rescue as a reason to look down on others. It was told to remember, and to let the memory make it kind: “You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (22:21). The Sabbath rest given to servants was grounded in the same memory: ‘Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt’ (Deuteronomy 5:15).

hard.line: The midwives refuse Pharaoh's order and give him a false answer. How the text treats their deception, and how readers differ.
Moses kills an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew. Was it justice or murder? What the text says, and what it leaves open.
‘I AM WHO I AM’: what the name means, and how it is also a promise to be with his people.
‘I will harden his heart’: the three ways Exodus says it, and the Reformed and Arminian readings.
‘A bridegroom of blood’: one of the most obscure passages in the Old Testament, and the main readings.
God says he was not known to the patriarchs by his name the LORD. How this fits Genesis.
The death of the firstborn announced: judgment, grief, and how readers have faced it.
The night of the death of the firstborn, told soberly, with grief for Egypt's dead.
‘About 600,000 men on foot’: the readings of the Hebrew word for ‘thousand’.
The crossing of the sea: where it happened, and how readers understand it.
Manna and the Sabbath, and where Christians differ on keeping a Sabbath today.
The Ten Commandments: how Jewish, Catholic and Lutheran, and Reformed and Orthodox traditions number them.
‘Visiting the iniquity of the fathers’: what it means beside Ezekiel 18, and what it does not mean.
Laws about servants and slaves: what they were, how they differ from later slavery, and their misuse.
‘Eye for eye’ as a limit for judges, and the readings of the law on harm to a pregnant woman.
The Levites and the sword after the golden calf.

words.line: ‘Names’, the Hebrew name of the book, from its first words: “These are the names of the sons of Israel” (1:1).
From the Greek exodos, a way out or departure. Luke uses the same word of Jesus' death in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31).
God's personal name, four Hebrew letters probably said ‘Yahweh’. English Bibles print it LORD in small capitals. Its meaning is opened in 3:14-15.
Hebrew ‘I am’ or ‘I will be’. God's name in 3:14 is ehyeh asher ehyeh, ‘I AM WHO I AM’; the same word promises ‘I will surely be with you’ (3:12).
To work or serve. The same word is used for slavery to Pharaoh and for the worship of God. Exodus is a change of masters.
To redeem: to buy back a relative from slavery, as next of kin. God uses it of himself in 6:6: “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm”.
Three Hebrew verbs: to make strong, to make heavy, and to make hard. The plague stories use all three of Pharaoh's heart (4:21; 7:14).
Passover, from the Hebrew verb meaning to pass over (12:13). The feast that remembers the night God spared Israel's houses.
Sea of reeds, the Hebrew name English Bibles give as the Red Sea (13:18). Where Israel crossed is not known.
‘Thousand’, but also a clan or a military unit (Judges 6:15). Behind the debate over the number who left Egypt (12:37).
Hebrew berit, a binding, sworn relationship with promises and duties on both sides. Sealed with blood at Sinai (24:8).
The tabernacle, from the verb ‘to dwell’. The tent where God lived among his people (25:8-9).
Glory, from a root meaning ‘heavy’ or ‘weighty’. The glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (40:34).
Loving devotion: loyal, covenant love that goes beyond what is owed. God names it as his own in 34:6-7.

timeline.what: The Hyksos, foreign rulers of northern Egypt for about a century, are driven out. Some scholars link the new king who did not know Joseph with the distrust of foreigners that followed.
Jacob's family multiplies in Egypt and is put to forced labor, building the store cities Pithom and Rameses (1:6-14).

timeline.when: About 1446 BC, on the early date
timeline.what: Israel leaves Egypt, counting back 480 years from Solomon's fourth year (1 Kings 6:1). Thutmose III or Amenhotep II would be the Pharaoh.
An Egyptian list at Soleb in Nubia, under Amenhotep III, names a land of the Shasu of Yhw, the earliest known name outside the Bible that looks like YHWH.
Ramesses II reigns. Many identify his Delta capital, Pi-Ramesses, with the store city Rameses (1:11).
Israel leaves Egypt, on the view that places the exodus under Ramesses II and reads the 480 years as a round number.
Israel arrives at Mount Sinai (19:1), where God gives the Ten Commandments and makes his covenant.
The tabernacle is set up on the first day of the first month of the second year, and God's glory fills it (40:17, 34).
Pharaoh Merneptah's victory stone names Israel as a people already in Canaan, the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible.
Many new villages appear in the hill country of Canaan, part of the case made for the later date.
Solomon begins the temple in his fourth year, ‘in the four hundred and eightieth year’ after the exodus (1 Kings 6:1).
A letter to the Jewish colony at Elephantine in Egypt gives the dates for the festival of unleavened bread, the earliest evidence of Passover outside the Bible.
The Torah is translated into Greek for Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt, the first part of the Septuagint.
The Nash Papyrus, a Hebrew sheet from Egypt, gives the Ten Commandments followed by the Shema.
The temple in Jerusalem is destroyed. Lambs can no longer be sacrificed, and the Seder becomes the Jewish form of Passover.
The pilgrim Egeria visits the mountain traditionally called Sinai and sees a church beside a bush at its foot.
The emperor Justinian builds the fortified monastery now called Saint Catherine's at the foot of Jebel Musa.
The spiritual Go Down, Moses is first published, from the singing of escaped slaves.
Édouard Naville excavates Tell el-Maskhuta in the valley east of the Delta and takes it to be Pithom.

places.name: Goshen
places.line: Where Jacob's family settled and Israel lived in Egypt, spared the flies and the hail (8:22; 9:26). Goshen is usually placed in the eastern Nile delta; it is drawn here roughly.

places.name: Canaan
places.line: The land God promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, ‘a land flowing with milk and honey’ (3:8; 6:4). Israel does not reach it in Exodus. Drawn roughly.

teaching.mapNote: Only two regions are drawn: Goshen, where Israel lived in Egypt, and Canaan, the land promised. Rameses, Succoth, the crossing of the sea and Mount Sinai are left off, because where they lay is debated, and no route is drawn, because the way Israel went is not known.
